Otolaryngology · published research

Vocal fatigue

No animal evidence was identified in the exact category.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

No animal evidence was identified in the exact category.

Summary of the Evidence

Three exact-category publications address vocal fatigue: one small randomized experiment in healthy adults, one uncontrolled teacher study, and one survey of speech-language pathologists. The survey reports practice or opinion rather than patient outcomes. None establishes lasting treatment benefit for a diagnosed voice disorder.

Human and clinical evidence

Kagan and Heaton randomized 16 healthy adults across four conditions after one hour of vocal loading: 828-nm near-infrared light, 628-nm red light, heat, or control. The red-light condition improved a combined pattern of phonation-threshold pressure, intensity-related measures, and relative fundamental frequency markers more than the comparison conditions (2017). The experiment measured short-term physiology after a standardized task, not relief of persistent fatigue in patients. Garrido et al. reported immediate pre/post changes in 41 teachers after a single uncontrolled treatment, with most changes in the severe-fatigue subgroup and no longer-term follow-up (2025). A survey of speech-language pathologists describes perceptions and use, not efficacy.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The randomized experiment used red and near-infrared LED conditions and a heat comparator after vocal loading. The red treatment warmed the neck to approximately 43.3 °C, so thermal effects may contribute to the observed response. The teacher report was uncontrolled and does not establish its own dose-response or durability. These protocols are not equivalent to ongoing clinical care for a voice disorder.

Interpretation

The evidence supports only a preliminary immediate physiological signal in a small healthy sample. Uncontrolled pre/post findings and clinician survey responses do not establish a clinical benefit for persistent vocal fatigue.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for immediate voice-function changes after vocal loading Very low for treatment of persistent voice symptoms
Publications and records3 exact-category records.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small randomized experiment in healthy adults found a short-term signal for selected voice markers with red light, while an uncontrolled teacher study and a professional survey do not establish treatment efficacy. A thermal response may have contributed to the red-light findings. Larger sham-controlled trials should measure symptoms and sustained work-related voice function.
